newsitem.title: NIGERIA: New Nigerian party calls for consensus, change.
newsitem.headline: New Nigerian party calls for consensus, change.

text.p: A newly registered Nigerian political party on Friday stressed consensus with the military government but said it hoped the promised democratic programme really would return the soldiers to the barracks.
At the Lagos convention of the Congress for National Consensus (CNC), the former chief executive of Guinness Breweries in Nigeria, Abel Ubeku, emerged as the party's chairman.
Ubeku, stressing the importance of consensus, added: "The word consensus means there must be disagreement which must be resolved amicably."
He urged delegates to mobilise for December municipal polls, which are viewed as a test of the strength of the new parties.
Jubril Aminu, a possible presidential candidate in 1998 from the CNC, said it was important that the stated transition programme was diligently implemented.
"Let us hope that the elections will come, will be free and fair, and be seen to be fair. This is very important," he said.

Political activity was banned by military ruler General Sani Abacha when he seized power in November 1993 in the aftermath of chaos unleashed by the annulment of a presidential poll meant to have ended a decade of army rule and restored democracy.

Abacha has set a programme of phased elections to hand over power to an elected president in October 1998 and an electoral commission recently registered five political parties -- but also turned down other applicants.

Abacha's critics say the democratic programme is a ruse for him to hang onto power. Among other things they point to the continued detention of opposition figures, including Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled vote.
They also say that the electoral commission refused to register political parties formed by well-known former politicians because Abacha wanted to clear the way for contesting the presidency.
Abacha has yet to comment on rumours he will stand in elections, like other other military men who have staged coups in West Africa have done.

"If the people of Nigeria want the head of state to contest an election it is left to them to ask him and it is absolutely his right to say yes or no," special duties minister Wada Nas, a close confidant of Abacha, told reporters on Thursday.
The newly registered United Nigeria Congress Party also held a convention on Thursday, electing as chairman Isa Mohammed, a former technocrat who served in the prior military government.

Western powers, keen for Africa's most populous nation to restore democracy quickly and respect civil liberties, are carefully monitoring Abacha's transition programme and have yet to comment on the evolving political scenario.
